newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK banks up for risky business amid property woes.
newsitem.headline: HK banks up for risky business amid property woes.

text.p: A slowdown in Hong Kong's real estate market may leave banks grappling with slow lending growth and tight margins, while efforts to reduce their property exposure may push them into riskier markets, analysts said.
"Going forward it is a bit more difficult operating environment," Shannon Garrett, investment analyst at SocGen Crosby Securities, said on Tuesday.
"It requires banks to look at different businesses which do have a higher element of risk," she said.
Hong Kong's incoming government is widely expected to impose measures to cool down rising real estate prices soon after the territory's return to Chinese rule at midnight of June 30.
"The rate of growth of mortgage lending will decrease," said Alex Wong, banking analyst at Dharmala Securities.
"It looks like banks are going to get more aggressive than before. We will see a deterioration in margins as competition gets more and more fierce," he said.
Mortgage margins are already under pressure, with most banks offering prime plus 25 basis points and some clients offered prime, analysts said.
"It is not a positive situation. People are going to be competing heavily on mortgage lending," said Thomas Monaco, a banking analyst at Bear Stearns.
"We are going to see decelerating earnings growth for the year," he said, predicting 1997 growth of about 14 percent for the sector and second-half growth of about 11 percent.
Mortgage lending has always been a major source of income for Hong Kong banks, but growing competition in the market has been driving the sector increasingly towards other areas.
The Hong Kong Monetary Authority, the territory's de facto central bank, is also encouraging banks to reduce their exposure to property as some banks push beyond a 40 percent guideline.
It said last month that additional lending restraints in mortgage lending policies may be required.

While analysts said they were not concerned about the high level of exposure, due to low default rates in Hong Kong and the establishment later this year of a Mortgage Corporation which would absorb part of banks' mortgage portfolio, they said they were worried about some diversification of businesses.

"The only way banks can really expand in areas other than mortgages tends to be by going into markets they have never been in. They end up having to increase their corporate activity where you are taking higher risk exposure," said Alan Hutcheson, a banking analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
Unsecured credit activities may be more lucrative than mortgage lending but are also higher risk, added Garrett.

"You are seeing a lot of talk about it right now with the government raising eyebrows at property exposure and mortgage lending exposure, and a lot of analysts raising warning flags saying diversifying away from property also means diversifying into higher risk business," she said.
But Wong said banks were moving into growth businesses.
"They will try to get into credit card and personal lending operations more aggressively. The margins are higher and there is higher potential for growth," he said.
Hutcheson said that mortgage growth was also at unsustainably high levels.
"Average values are going to continue going up, so having fewer units per year but an average price a little higher each year is not a particularly bad situation for banks," he said.
